Match floors

Areas

Loading areas — where the floor's capacity differs. Auto-trace reads them off the load map, or copy them from a floor you have already done. By hand: Draw loading area and click the corners, or press F and click inside an outlined area to fill it.

Slab conditions — draw only where the floor differs from its level baseline: a slab of another thickness or T.O.S., an opening with no slab, a beam stem, or the floor edge. A slab area can be switched to on grade in its Type box. The floor edge itself is settled on the Building step; Auto detect reads beams and openings only inside it.

While drawing — hold Shift for ortho, or leave the Ortho toggle on; double-click or Enter finishes the shape. Closing a shape puts the caret in its first field, Enter/Tab move on and the last one returns to the plan, and the tool stays armed for the next shape until you press Esc.

Editing — click a shape to select it; drag corners, Shift+click a corner to remove it, Alt+click an edge to add one. Esc backs out of whatever you are doing, one step at a time.

Moving a shape — drag a shape that is already selected; a press inside an unselected one only selects it, so a wobble cannot nudge your markup. Snapping catches the corner nearest where you grabbed it, so you can drop that corner on a grid crossing; hold Shift mid-drag to keep the move square.

How they are read — a floor with a floor edge exists only inside it; one without exists everywhere. Where loading areas overlap, the smaller area cuts out of the larger one and governs its own space.

Where the concrete goes — the floor edge decides it on the floor being poured. With no edge drawn, its loading areas and its slab areas together are the extent, so a slab drawn on the slab layer is poured even where no loading area covers it. An opening always punches out; a beam adds nothing on its own.

The typical capacity covers everywhere no area is drawn. Set it above and draw areas only where the floor differs from it — a floor with a floor edge and a typical capacity needs no areas at all. The floor being poured needs no capacity of its own; it applies the load rather than carrying it.

Auto detect

Read what is on the drawing, inside the confirmed floor edge, and offer it for review. Nothing is written until you accept it.

Copy areas from another floor

Areas are carried over in building feet through both floors' matches, so they land in the right place even when the sheets differ. The copies are independent afterward — edit them freely. One undo step.

How capacity is worked out
  • capacity = SDL + 1.6/1.3 × LL, with × 0.6 on the live load where it is reduced per code. Rounded down.
  • This drawing does not say which live loads were reduced, so every row starts assumed reduced (the safe reading) and stays flagged until you confirm it against the structural capacity chart.
  • The grey figure beside each capacity is what it would be on the other basis. Editing a value or ticking the box confirms that row.
How capacity is worked out
  • An area tagged C2 takes live load C and dead load 2: capacity = SDL + 1.6/1.3 × LL, with × 0.6 on the live load where the drawing prints (R). Rounded down.
  • Reduction is read from the drawing, so nothing here is assumed. Edit a value only if the drawing was misread.

Source & assumptions
  • Titan HV post shores (#1–#5, XL 625) from Reshore Post Data.pdf, MCC version, 3:1 safety factor, updated 1/10/2022. Every value verified against that chart.
  • HV Load Chart ratings only. The chart's higher “Plate to Plate per SSFI” ratings are deliberately excluded.
  • HV chart assumes unlaced shores with main beams loaded on both sides of the drop head. The chart requires a 20% reduction if loaded on one side only — not applied here; allow for it yourself where that condition exists.
  • Listed heights include the 10" drop head, so they are compared directly against shore clear height.
  • Ellis 4×4 shores use the unbraced allowable-load curve. Bracing at midpoint or third points permits more — not modelled.
  • Shores must be plumb and bear on concrete. Mudsill conditions need Titan engineering.
  • Stiff shores on slab on grade (anything not ticked Wood): a chain of steel or aluminum posts from the pour down to grade holds the slabs flat, so they cannot deflect and take their share and the bottom shores carry the full stack. Every such base gets a wood pad — two layers of ¾" plywood (1½" min), 12"×12" or larger — and the results flag every row where this applies.
